newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Weak rand sorts SAfrica textile winners and losers.
newsitem.headline: Weak rand sorts SAfrica textile winners and losers.

text.p: The sharp fall in the rand, notably against the British pound, is separating out the export winners from the losers in South Africa's tattered clothing industry.

The winners are those companies that are making high value-added clothing such as jackets, trousers, men's suits and quality knitwear and exporting them to Britain, against whose currency the rand has reached all-time lows.
The losers are those companies concentrating mainly on the weak domestic market or exporting low value items such as ladies' underwear.
"The only way that you make money out of exports is to have value-added production," said BOE Natwest Securities analyst Syd Vianello.
And if the companies had been paid in sterling, which had moved from 5.72 rands to the pound since September 1995 to around 7.90 rands now, their returns would have "increased dramatically", he said.
"I wish more were moving into high value-added, but they are not."
Those that had taken the high value-added route included Rex Trueform, Towles, Edgar Jacobs Ltd and Pals Holdings, he said.

Pals chairman and joint managing director Selwyn Kagan told Reuters that this put paid to allegations by some that the phasing out of the general export incentive scheme (GEIS) would adversely affect export profitability in the clothing sector.
GEIS, a cash payment based on FOB export values, has been taxed since April 1995 and in July last year was cut from 12 to six percent. It is expected to be phased out at the end of 1997.
"Incentives are becoming worth less and less, but at the same time the rand is depreciating and one can still afford to export," Kagan said.
Pals exports jackets and trousers to Britain, where its main customer is the Littlewoods group.
The domestic clothing industry has been hard hit by illegal imports, high import duties for cloth, weak domestic demand and an illegal seven-day strike in 1996.

Bernard Richards, Clothing Federation of South Africa chairman and managing director of Seardel Investment Corp, in November urged the government to implement a wide range of promised incentives which he claimed could double clothing exports in two years.

Most of the so-called "supply side" measures concentrate on training and improving productivity rather than tax-based incentives. Vianello said it was highly unlikely that tax-based incentives would ever be offered.
"They (the government) are saying: the currency is where you will make your money. The currency will fall to a level where your exports become competitive," he said.
